name: Ethiosemitic
region: The highlands of Ethiopia and Eritrea
defining_innovation: The Semitic languages of the Horn of Africa, shaped by long contact with Cushitic: verb-final word order, and in Amharic the loss of most of the old guttural consonants.

chapters.title: Origins
chapters.body:
About a dozen Semitic languages are spoken in Ethiopia and Eritrea, including Amharic, one of the most widely spoken Semitic languages after Arabic, and Tigrinya. Their ancestors are generally thought to have crossed from southern Arabia in the first millennium BCE, around the time South Arabian-style inscriptions appear in the Ethiopian highlands. Some scholars argue for an earlier or more gradual presence. Kitchen and colleagues' computational study (2009) estimated a single arrival around 800 BCE.

In Africa, Ethiosemitic speakers lived among speakers of Cushitic languages, and the contact reshaped them. Most Ethiosemitic languages put the verb at the end of the clause, a Cushitic pattern and not a Semitic one. They also realise the Semitic 'emphatic' consonants as ejectives (`tʼ`, `sʼ`, `kʼ`), which some scholars think was the original Proto-Semitic pronunciation.

chapters.title: Ge'ez and Its Script
chapters.body: **Ge'ez** was the language of the kingdom of Aksum. It was first written in a consonantal script taken from South Arabian. In the 4th century, in the inscriptions of King **Ezana**, who adopted Christianity, vowel markings attached to each consonant appeared, turning the script into the Ethiopic *fidäl*. Each character stands for a consonant plus a vowel. Ge'ez ceased to be spoken some time in the late first or early second millennium CE, but it remains the liturgical language of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches, much as Latin was in the West.

chapters.title: Amharic
chapters.body: Amharic rose with the Solomonic dynasty from the 13th century as the language of the royal court (*lǝssanä nǝguś*, 'the king's tongue'), and it is now Ethiopia's federal working language. It has moved further from its Semitic roots than its northern relatives Tigrinya and Tigre: it has lost or merged most of the old guttural consonants, and it takes a good deal of vocabulary and grammar from Cushitic neighbours. It is still written in the Ge'ez *fidäl*.

speakers.note: Amharic has about 35 million first-language speakers and Tigrinya about 9 million; Ge'ez survives only in liturgy, and some small languages such as Gafat are extinct.

sources.citation: Eberhard, David M., Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig, eds. 2024. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 27th ed. Dallas: SIL International.

sample.translation: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name (the Lord's Prayer, Matthew 6:9)

sources.citation: Matthew 6:9, Ge'ez text as used in the daily prayers of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches.

turning_points.title: Across the Red Sea
turning_points.description: Semitic speakers from southern Arabia settle in the Ethiopian highlands, and Ethiosemitic begins its separate history. Whether this was one migration, several, or a longer process of contact is debated.

sources.citation: Kitchen, Andrew, Christopher Ehret, Shiferaw Assefa & Connie J. Mulligan. 2009. Bayesian phylogenetic analysis of Semitic languages identifies an Early Bronze Age origin of Semitic in the Near East. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 276.
Weninger, Stefan, ed. 2011. The Semitic Languages: An International Handbook. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.

turning_points.title: Cushitic neighbours
turning_points.description: Long bilingualism with Cushitic languages such as Agaw and Oromo gives Ethiosemitic verb-final word order, new vocabulary and, in the southern languages especially, Cushitic sound patterns.

sources.citation: Weninger, Stefan, ed. 2011. The Semitic Languages: An International Handbook. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.

turning_points.title: The vocalised Ge'ez script
turning_points.description: Under King Ezana of Aksum, the consonantal script inherited from South Arabian gains systematic vowel markings attached to each consonant and becomes the Ethiopic *fidäl*, still used for Amharic, Tigrinya and Ge'ez.

sources.citation: Hetzron, Robert, ed. 1997. The Semitic Languages. London: Routledge.

turning_points.title: Ge'ez becomes a church language
turning_points.description: Ge'ez stops being spoken and survives as the language of liturgy and scholarship, while Tigrinya, Tigre and Amharic become the spoken languages. The date is uncertain because the written language hardly changed.

sources.citation: Weninger, Stefan, ed. 2011. The Semitic Languages: An International Handbook. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.

turning_points.date: Before the earliest Amharic texts (14th century CE)
turning_points.title: Amharic loses the gutturals
turning_points.description: The pharyngeal and laryngeal consonants inherited from Semitic (`ʕ ḥ h ʔ`) are lost or merged in Amharic, although Ge'ez spelling still writes them. Tigrinya keeps them. Cushitic influence is often suggested as the cause.

sources.citation: Hetzron, Robert, ed. 1997. The Semitic Languages. London: Routledge.
